doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

chapter: Jazz, Lincoln Center and the music market
title: Missing middle of the jazz market and the tribute-album trend
summary: He says booking splits between a few stars and low-paid players with little between. He complains about tribute concerts and centennials, and Davern called it necrophilia.

bands.name: Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Coleman. There’s a handful. But there’s not. So if you don’t have giants then you’ve got people that are just being marketed very well. And if that becomes sort of your top tier, and everybody else is kind of on the bottom, there’s this huge hole in the middle. There’s $5,000 and less, and $50,000 and more. But in between it’s a little tricky. And I don’t know if that was intentional.

The market has definitely changed as a result of their kind of — and it’s also changed the marketing of the music and the make-up of what’s being marketed. I’m tired of looking in the jazz magazines and seeing everything is a freaking tribute to something else. Like really? I had somebody want to do that recently. They were going to do a repertory concert. You know, of the Hot Fives and Sevens. Well you don’t want me for that, trust me. This was the Benny Goodman centennial, which for me, the best thing about the Benny Goodman centennial was that we’re only a year away from the Artie Shaw centennial. But that’s the best thing for me. But it’s just, even albums. I mean really? There’s a conservatism about that that concerns me. I mean Kenny would be much more blatant about it. He’d call it necrophilia. And I don’t necessarily entirely disagree.
